newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: NATO set to table CFE arms control proposal.
newsitem.headline: NATO set to table CFE arms control proposal.

text.p: NATO allies prepared on Thursday to present proposals for reducing conventional forces in Europe to a Vienna security summit in a bid to assuage Russian concerns over its plans to expand the alliance eastwards.
"The proposal supplied by NATO members will be tabled at the body dealing with Conventional Forces in Europe (CFE) at 1630 (1530 GMT) this afternoon," a diplomatic source said.
"Then on Tuesday a working group will start negotiations on adapting the treaty, looking at the NATO and Russian views," the source added.
The NATO allies on Wednesday agreed comprehensive changes to the 1990 CFE arms control treaty, taking account of several Russian objections to existing ceilings on arsenals.

The original CFE treaty was negotiated under the auspices of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe, to try to strike a balance between the military hardware held by the NATO military alliance and the now-defunct Soviet-led Warsaw pact.

NATO sources have said U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright on her visit to Moscow would simultaneously unveil the proposal to Russian leaders as part of a package of measures designed to win Russian acquiescence to NATO enlargement.

NATO has raised Moscow's shackles with its plan to admit former Soviet satellites, starting with Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic. The alliance was created during the Cold War era to defend the West from attack by the Soviet Union.
Russia was the only one of the CFE signatories that failed to meet a November 17, 1995 deadline to destroy pieces of its military equipment, citing fears it would jeopardise its defence capacities.
The CFE states agreed in Vienna last June to extend the CFE deadline, giving Russia until May 31, 1999 to meet its arms cuts quotas.

The new NATO position clearly accepts the principle of limits on the arsenals of individual countries as opposed to regions. "This makes sure that Russia does not face off against NATO as a bloc," one alliance source said on Wednesday.

The alliance has also accepted Russia's insistence on having "territorial" rather than "national" limits, which effectively prevents NATO from massing troops in one particular area near Russia's borders.
Albright's package of sweeteners also includes a proposal to create a joint NATO-Russia peacekeeping force and an offer of close consultation within the alliance's command structure.

NATO is due to invite new countries to join the alliance at a special summit in Madrid in July. Albright said she wanted entry negotiations to be completed by December to allow two years for ratification by national parliaments.
